title: LuminaAI x Redwood — POC scoping (batching tiers + success metrics)
topics: Choosing batching tier per route (chat streaming vs non-streaming vs embeddings)
Latency SLO definitions and measurement windows
Cost metrics ($/1M tokens) and throughput targets
Dashboards and alerting required during pilot
summary: LuminaAI and Redwood scoped a 2–3 week pilot to evaluate workload-aware batching tiers (fast/standard/cost-efficient) per API route. LuminaAI will run streaming chat for end-user UI plus non-streaming summarization jobs and embeddings. They aligned on preliminary per-route tier defaults (fast for streaming chat, standard for non-streaming chat, cost-efficient for async summarization) with explicit success metrics (p95 latency, stream token cadence, timeout/cancel rate, and $/1M tokens). Redwood will provide required dashboards/alerts (latency by tier, queue delay, batch formation stats, GPU util, overload/backpressure signals) and a monitoring checklist, plus guidance on viewing effective config/overrides.
next_steps: Redwood (Alex) to send a proposed tier-by-route matrix and minimal config snippets for Python/TS SDK by 2025-03-03
LuminaAI (Priya/Evan) to share current traffic shape: prompt length histogram, concurrency estimate, and % streaming vs non-streaming by 2025-03-04
Redwood (Sean) to confirm alert thresholds for p95/p99 and queue-delay noisy-metric handling and share dashboard links for pilot by 2025-03-05
LuminaAI (Karthik) to identify on-call escalation channel + who will watch dashboards during ramp by 2025-03-05
Schedule a 30-min technical check-in after first benchmark run (target week of 2025-03-10)
action_items: Alex Martinez (Redwood): send SDK config examples for batching_tier and how to override max_queue_delay without breaking tier selection
Nikhil Sharma (Redwood): provide Hosted API behavior notes for streaming cadence expectations under fast tier and what headers/metrics are exposed
Sean Gallagher (Redwood): provide pilot SLO doc excerpt + recommended alerts (timeout rate, queue delay, cancel rate) and rollback triggers
Priya Deshmukh (LuminaAI): confirm whether pilot will be Hosted first or needs Dedicated from day 1 due to data isolation
Evan Lin (LuminaAI): share representative prompts and a small prompt set for regression checks (10–20) including tool-call-ish formats if applicable
questions: Can LuminaAI choose different tiers per route (e.g., /chat vs /embeddings) and per environment (staging vs prod)?
What is the expected impact of cost-efficient tier on streaming token cadence and first-token latency?
Which metrics does Redwood expose for queue delay and batch formation, and can LuminaAI alert on them?
How does explicit batching config interact with tier defaults (precedence / effective config visibility)?
What are the rollback signals and how quickly can Redwood pause a ramp?
transcript:
Meeting: LuminaAI x Redwood — POC scoping (batching tiers + success metrics)
Recorded: Feb 28, 2025 9:00 AM PT
Duration: 49:03
Attendees:
- Miguel Santos (Redwood)
- Alex Martinez (Redwood)
- Nikhil Sharma (Redwood)
- Sean Gallagher (Redwood)
- Sarah Nguyen (LuminaAI)
- Evan Lin (LuminaAI)
- Priya Deshmukh (LuminaAI)
- Karthik Iyer (LuminaAI)

[00:00] Miguel Santos: Cool, I think we’re live. Thanks everyone for making time. This one is mostly POC scoping — like what are we testing, how do we pick the batching tiers per route, and what do you all need in terms of dashboards and alerts so you’re comfortable.

[00:16] Sarah Nguyen: Yep, sounds good.

[00:18] Miguel Santos: Quick intros and then we’ll jump. I’m Miguel, I run the account on the Redwood side. Alex is solutions, Nikhil is on the Hosted API side, and Sean is SRE — he’s gonna keep us honest on SLOs and alerting.

[00:30] Priya Deshmukh: I’m Priya, platform eng at LuminaAI.

[00:33] Evan Lin: Evan, ML engineer.

[00:35] Karthik Iyer: Karthik, SRE.

[00:37] Sarah Nguyen: Sarah PM.

[00:40] Miguel Santos: Great. Sarah, do you want to set context? Like what “success” looks like for the pilot.

[00:47] Sarah Nguyen: Sure. We have two main product surfaces. One is our end-user “assistant” UI, it’s streaming chat — people hate lag, obviously. The other is behind-the-scenes summarization and labeling jobs. That’s non-streaming, can be async. And then embeddings for retrieval.

[01:06] Sarah Nguyen: We’re looking at Redwood mainly because we don’t want to keep tuning vLLM knobs ourselves. We also use OpenAI today for some traffic, and we’ve looked at Bedrock. Cost is a big driver but we can’t blow up latency.

[01:21] Miguel Santos: Yep. This maps exactly to why we’re doing the tiered batching defaults.

[01:26] Alex Martinez: And the POC is basically: can we set tiers per route — fast, standard, cost-efficient — and have it behave predictably without you having to babysit max batch size and queue delay.

[01:39] Evan Lin: The “per route” thing — is that literally per endpoint? Like /chat/completions versus /embeddings.

[01:44] Nikhil Sharma: Yes. In Redwood config you can set it per route and per model. So chat streaming could be “fast”, embeddings could be “standard” or “cost-efficient” depending on your tolerance.

[01:57] Priya Deshmukh: And if we don’t set anything, what happens.

[02:00] Nikhil Sharma: During beta it’ll be opt-in. So default stays as today unless you choose a tier.

[02:06] Miguel Santos: For the POC we’d recommend being explicit so measurement is clean.

[02:11] Sean Gallagher: +1. Otherwise you can’t attribute changes to the tier.

[02:15] Sarah Nguyen: So can we talk recommended mapping? Like what would you suggest for our three workloads.

[02:22] Alex Martinez: Let’s break it down:
1) Streaming chat (UI)
2) Non-streaming chat (maybe internal or some API)
3) Async summarization (bulk jobs)
4) Embeddings

[02:33] Alex Martinez: Streaming chat generally wants “fast”. It minimizes queue delay and tends to prioritize decode so your token cadence stays stable.

[02:43] Evan Lin: When you say token cadence, you mean like tokens per second? Or first token latency.

[02:47] Alex Martinez: Both matter. For streaming we usually look at TTFT (time to first token) and then steady-state tokens/sec (or time between chunks). “Fast” is tuned for that.

[02:58] Sean Gallagher: Practically, if we see queue delay creeping up, cadence gets jittery even if average throughput is good.

[03:07] Karthik Iyer: We’ve seen that — when batching gets aggressive you get bursty updates.

[03:12] Nikhil Sharma: Exactly. We had a regression internally where fast tier got too batchy and cadence was choppy — we fixed it by weighting decode higher. That’s part of why we’re instrumenting it.

[03:25] Sarah Nguyen: Okay, so streaming chat = fast.

[03:28] Alex Martinez: Yup.

[03:30] Alex Martinez: Non-streaming chat — if it’s user-facing but not streamed, standard is usually fine. If it’s async, cost-efficient is okay.

[03:39] Priya Deshmukh: Summarization job is async and we run it overnight mostly. We care about total spend and not timing out.

[03:47] Sean Gallagher: For that, cost-efficient tier is the right starting point, but we will set guardrails so error rates don’t climb. It tends to allow higher queue delay and larger batches.

[03:59] Evan Lin: Our biggest fear is tail latency and timeouts. We currently have a 30 second gateway timeout in one place.

[04:06] Sean Gallagher: Good callout. For the POC we should write down your client timeout and server timeout so we don’t accidentally “optimize cost” by pushing you into timeout territory.

[04:15] Miguel Santos: Can you share the exact timeouts per workload?

[04:18] Priya Deshmukh: UI is 60 seconds overall, but we start streaming within like 1.5 seconds or the user bails. For async, our job runner is 5 minutes, but we cap per request at 90 seconds right now.

[04:34] Alex Martinez: Great, that helps.

[04:37] Sarah Nguyen: For embeddings, we do it in real time sometimes on document ingest. Latency matters but it’s not user staring at it.

[04:46] Evan Lin: It is like batchy. We can run multiple texts.

[04:49] Alex Martinez: Embeddings is usually a throughput play. Standard tier is a safe default; cost-efficient can work if your p95 can tolerate more queue delay.

[05:00] Karthik Iyer: We’ll probably want standard for embeddings at first so we don’t complicate.

[05:05] Miguel Santos: That’s reasonable. So draft matrix:
- /chat streaming: fast
- /chat non-streaming: standard
- /summarize (async job route): cost-efficient
- /embeddings: standard

[05:18] Sarah Nguyen: Sounds right.

[05:20] Evan Lin: But we might do tool calls. Like the assistant sometimes emits JSON and we call tools.

[05:26] Nikhil Sharma: Tool calling itself doesn’t change batching directly, but you’ll see different prompt length distribution and stop/start patterns. The workload-aware part uses signals like prompt length buckets and concurrency.

[05:39] Evan Lin: Are those “signals” something we have to send? Or you just infer.

[05:43] Alex Martinez: You don’t send. It’s observed in the runtime.

[05:46] Priya Deshmukh: So then what does “workload-aware” mean in practice? Like it will pick different max batch size depending on prompt length?

[05:55] Alex Martinez: Basically yes. It’s not bespoke per customer yet, but within a tier it adjusts parameters to avoid pathological cases. Example: if prompts are long-context, prefill dominates, and it might tighten queue delay to avoid huge prefill stalls.

[06:11] Sean Gallagher: And we’ll cap KV cache pressure; cost-efficient is where people can OOM if you go too wide at high concurrency.

[06:18] Karthik Iyer: Yeah, the OOM thing scares me.

[06:21] Sean Gallagher: It should be guarded. During pilot we’ll watch memory pressure metrics and cancel/timeout rates.

[06:29] Miguel Santos: Let’s talk success metrics. We typically define 3 buckets:
1) Latency SLO adherence
2) Cost per token / per 1M tokens
3) Reliability: timeouts, 5xx, cancel rates

[06:42] Sarah Nguyen: For the UI, we care about p95 and maybe p99. But also TTFT.

[06:48] Alex Martinez: Yep. We can track TTFT p50/p95 for streaming and also inter-chunk delay.

[06:55] Evan Lin: We also look at “tokens per second” in our app. But it’s noisy.

[06:59] Nikhil Sharma: It is noisy, but we can use a cadence metric like “time between streamed events” and “decode throughput” server-side. We have spans for prefill and decode.

[07:11] Priya Deshmukh: For the async summarization, I mostly care about dollars and that it doesn’t blow up long tail.

[07:18] Sean Gallagher: For async we can set a looser p95 target, but define an absolute timeout budget. Like p99 < 80s, and error rate < 0.5%.

[07:30] Karthik Iyer: What about queue delay? We’ve had issues where queue delay is the hidden killer.

[07:35] Sean Gallagher: We will explicitly dashboard “queue_delay_ms” as its own histogram. Alerting is tricky because it can be noisy, but for pilot we can add a threshold: e.g., p95 queue delay above X for 10 minutes.

[07:50] Alex Martinez: And also batch formation stats: average batch size, max batch size observed, batch wait time.

[07:56] Evan Lin: Is that per model or per route.

[07:58] Alex Martinez: Both — labels include route, model, tier, region.

[08:05] Sarah Nguyen: Can we see those dashboards ourselves? Or only Redwood.

[08:10] Miguel Santos: For Hosted, we can give you a customer-facing view in Console for key metrics. Some deep internals are Redwood-only today, but we can export or share reports during pilot.

[08:22] Priya Deshmukh: We need something that our SRE team can actually use. Like if latency spikes, we need to know if it’s queue delay versus model issue.

[08:30] Sean Gallagher: Totally. Minimum dashboards I’d propose:
- Latency: p50/p95/p99 end-to-end by route/model/tier
- Streaming: TTFT and token cadence distribution
- Queueing: queue delay histogram + time in scheduler
- Batch formation: batch size distribution, batch wait time
- GPU utilization and memory/KV cache pressure (if Dedicated; limited in Hosted)
- Errors: timeout rate, cancellations, 429/backpressure, 5xx

[08:55] Karthik Iyer: We also need alert routes/ownership. Who gets paged if this is pilot.

[09:00] Miguel Santos: During pilot, Redwood will monitor and you’ll monitor. But we’ll define escalation. Typically, you ping a shared Slack channel and we have on-call SRE backing it.

[09:12] Sarah Nguyen: What are the “rollback triggers” in your world.

[09:16] Sean Gallagher: For tier rollout: if p95 latency regresses above threshold (say 15% for fast tier), or timeouts increase above baseline +0.2%, or queue delay p99 exceeds a hard cap for sustained window, we pause ramp.

[09:32] Alex Martinez: Also if streaming cadence degrades — users complain even if p95 isn’t terrible.

[09:38] Evan Lin: How would you detect cadence degrade automatically?

[09:41] Nikhil Sharma: We track inter-chunk gap percentiles. If p95 inter-chunk gap blows out, that’s a red flag.

[09:49] Priya Deshmukh: That’s really useful.

[09:52] Miguel Santos: Cool. On cost metrics — do you care about $/1M tokens? Or total monthly spend.

[09:58] Sarah Nguyen: For pilot, $/1M tokens and also “cost per summary” would be nice.

[10:05] Alex Martinez: We can do $/1M output tokens or total tokens. Usually customers like $/1M total tokens (input+output) for comparability.

[10:14] Evan Lin: We also want throughput, like summaries per hour.

[10:17] Sean Gallagher: Throughput is a good secondary metric. But don’t optimize it at the cost of tail latency unless it’s truly async.

[10:24] Karthik Iyer: Can you talk about percent ramp? Like do we flip it on for everyone at once.

[10:29] Miguel Santos: No, we’ll do staged. For Hosted, we can gate by model/region and percentage of traffic. Typically: 1% → 5% → 25% → 50% and stop if any guardrail triggers.

[10:44] Priya Deshmukh: Can we control it by route? Like only summarization first.

[10:49] Alex Martinez: Yes, do it route by route. That’s less risky.

[10:53] Sarah Nguyen: We’d like to start with summarization and embeddings, then do UI chat last.

[10:59] Miguel Santos: That’s a great plan. Lower risk first.

[11:02] Evan Lin: Wait, for embeddings— are you batching across different customers? Is there data leakage.

[11:08] Nikhil Sharma: In Hosted, batching is within isolation boundaries — we don’t mix tenant data in a single batch. The runtime keeps request isolation per customer. We can share details in security doc.

[11:20] Priya Deshmukh: We might still need Dedicated eventually because of contracts. Not today, but soon.

[11:26] Miguel Santos: Understood. Let’s keep POC in Hosted for speed, and we can scope Dedicated as phase 2.

[11:33] Karthik Iyer: If we do Hosted, what about data retention.

[11:36] Nikhil Sharma: Default is no training; logs are limited; we can configure retention. For POC we can enable stricter logging and you can opt out of payload logging.

[11:48] Sean Gallagher: For dashboards, we mostly need metadata metrics, not payload.

[11:52] Sarah Nguyen: Okay.

[11:54] Alex Martinez: Let’s get specific on targets per tier, for your pilot. We can propose:
- Streaming chat (fast): TTFT p95 <= 1.2s (or whatever baseline), end-to-end p95 <= 3.5s for typical 200 output tokens; inter-chunk gap p95 <= 250ms
- Standard (non-stream/embeddings): end-to-end p95 within baseline +10%, error rate <= baseline
- Cost-efficient (summaries): $/1M tokens improvement >= 15% with p95 latency regression <= 20% and no increase in timeouts

[12:27] Evan Lin: The “typical 200 output tokens” is hard; ours varies.

[12:31] Alex Martinez: Fair. We can normalize by token count: use “ms per output token” and track TTFT separately.

[12:40] Sean Gallagher: And we’ll bucket by prompt length. Like 0–512, 512–2k, 2k–8k, etc. Otherwise long-context outliers distort.

[12:50] Priya Deshmukh: We can provide prompt length histograms. We have it in Datadog.

[12:55] Miguel Santos: Perfect. Please share those.

[12:58] Evan Lin: For summarization, we often do like 6–10k input tokens.

[13:04] Nikhil Sharma: That’s exactly where batching gets tricky. Prefill dominates and naive batching can cause long stalls. The tier defaults will be more conservative on queue delay when it detects long prompts.

[13:18] Evan Lin: So it’s dynamic within the tier.

[13:20] Alex Martinez: Yep. Still within safety rails.

[13:23] Karthik Iyer: What about alerts. I want concrete thresholds for the POC.

[13:28] Sean Gallagher: We can draft, but we need your baseline. For week 1, do “informational” alerts and then tighten. Roughly:
- Timeout rate > 0.5% over 10m (page)
- 5xx error rate > 0.2% over 10m (page)
- p95 latency regression > 15% vs control for 15m (page)
- p99 queue delay > 500ms for fast tier sustained 10m (warn/page depending)
- Cancel rate spikes (warn)

[13:59] Priya Deshmukh: Is cancel rate like client disconnects?

[14:02] Nikhil Sharma: Client disconnects and server-side admission control drops. We label reasons.

[14:08] Evan Lin: Admission control is basically load shedding.

[14:11] Sean Gallagher: Yes — and the reason codes matter. If we see “overload_cost_efficient_queue” or something, that tells us it’s the tier parameters interacting with backpressure.

[14:24] Alex Martinez: For cost-efficient, overload protection is key. Otherwise you get the “it’s cheap but it times out” scenario.

[14:32] Sarah Nguyen: That’s like the nightmare scenario.

[14:36] Miguel Santos: Totally.

[14:38] Sarah Nguyen: Another question: can we set cost-efficient tier only for certain orgs? Like our free tier.

[14:44] Alex Martinez: Policy-wise yes, you can route based on headers or customer tier. For POC, keep it simple: route based on endpoint.

[14:52] Priya Deshmukh: We can do that later.

[14:55] Evan Lin: How do we debug effective config? Like if we set tier = standard but also have max batch size somewhere, which wins.

[15:03] Nikhil Sharma: Explicit knobs override tier defaults. Tier is like a recommended preset. If you set a specific max_queue_delay, that will take precedence.

[15:12] Evan Lin: That can get confusing.

[15:14] Alex Martinez: Agreed. We have an “explain config” view coming where you can see computed defaults vs overrides. For pilot, we can share the effective config output in Console.

[15:26] Priya Deshmukh: We will need that, because we have some legacy config.

[15:31] Miguel Santos: We’ll make it part of the POC checklist: confirm “effective tier” and no unintended overrides.

[15:39] Karthik Iyer: Can you export config as JSON? We want to version it.

[15:43] Nikhil Sharma: Yes, you can export config; audit logs for changes are in enterprise, but we can still provide change history during POC.

[15:55] Sarah Nguyen: Okay, timeline. We want this in March.

[15:59] Miguel Santos: Proposed timeline: next week you share traffic shape, we configure staging, week after we run benchmarks and ramp cost-efficient for summarization at low %, then standard for embeddings, then fast tier for streaming last.

[16:15] Priya Deshmukh: That’s fine.

[16:17] Evan Lin: Benchmarks—are we doing synthetic or replay.

[16:20] Alex Martinez: Ideally both. For quick iteration: synthetic corpus based on your histograms. Then a small replay with anonymized prompts if possible.

[16:31] Sarah Nguyen: We can’t share raw prompts broadly.

[16:34] Miguel Santos: Understood. You can provide a small prompt set with scrubbed content and we can still validate the tier behavior. Also Redwood can run perf canary style tests internally.

[16:47] Evan Lin: We also care about quality regressions. Batching shouldn’t change outputs but sampling can make it look different.

[16:55] Nikhil Sharma: Right. If you’re using non-deterministic sampling, differences might appear. For the pilot, use fixed seed where possible or deterministic settings for comparison runs.

[17:06] Evan Lin: We can do temperature 0 for summarization baseline.

[17:09] Sarah Nguyen: UI is temp 0.7 though.

[17:11] Alex Martinez: For UI, measure latency and UX; don’t over-index on exact token match.

[17:18] Karthik Iyer: Back to dashboards: do we get per-tier breakdown. Because if we A/B, I need to see tier label.

[17:25] Sean Gallagher: Yes. Tier is a label on metrics. Also include region, model, route.

[17:33] Priya Deshmukh: What about multi-region. We’re mostly us-east.

[17:36] Miguel Santos: For pilot, keep single region to avoid confounding. Later we can test failover.

[17:44] Sarah Nguyen: We also want to know “how to opt out” if something breaks.

[17:49] Miguel Santos: Opt-out is immediate: set tier to standard or remove tier selection, and we can drop traffic back to baseline. Also we can pause feature flag at the control plane.

[18:03] Evan Lin: Is this per request header? Or config only.

[18:07] Nikhil Sharma: For now, it’s config. You can also set header-based routing but that’s advanced.

[18:15] Priya Deshmukh: Okay.

[18:17] Alex Martinez: Let’s capture the exact POC success criteria in writing. Sarah, what do you want to report up to leadership.

[18:25] Sarah Nguyen: Basically: “We can reduce spend X% on summarization without hurting reliability, and UI latency is stable or improved.” Also “we have good operational visibility.”

[18:39] Miguel Santos: Great. So we’ll define:
- Summarization: >=15% cost reduction ($/1M total tokens) with timeout rate not worse than baseline
- Streaming UI: TTFT p95 no worse than baseline, and cadence p95 stable
- Ops: dashboards + alerts exist and our SRE is comfortable

[18:56] Karthik Iyer: Add that we can page Redwood during pilot.

[18:59] Miguel Santos: 100%.

[19:01] Sean Gallagher: And explicitly: no tail explosions. We can set a p99 cap.

[19:07] Evan Lin: p99 is tricky because low volume.

[19:10] Sean Gallagher: Then use p95 plus max observed and a minimum sample size.

[19:15] Alex Martinez: During ramp we’ll keep traffic low until we have enough samples.

[19:21] Priya Deshmukh: Are there any known limitations with cost-efficient tier.

[19:25] Nikhil Sharma: It can increase queue delay and that can trigger client timeouts if your timeouts are tight. Also on very long context, if concurrency is high, KV cache pressure can spike. That’s why we watch memory and cancellations.

[19:43] Evan Lin: How do you prevent OOM.

[19:45] Sean Gallagher: Hard limits + admission control. And we tune per model family.

[19:50] Alex Martinez: During pilot, we can start with conservative parameters even within cost-efficient tier.

[19:57] Sarah Nguyen: So cost-efficient isn’t always the cheapest.

[20:00] Alex Martinez: It’s the best default to reduce unit cost, but if it causes timeouts then total cost can go up. That’s why the guardrails.

[20:12] Miguel Santos: Exactly.

[20:14] Karthik Iyer: Okay, last thing: what do you need from us right now.

[20:18] Miguel Santos: Two things:
1) Traffic shape / histograms (prompt length, output length, concurrency, % streaming)
2) Confirm which routes we’ll test first and what the success thresholds are.

[20:32] Priya Deshmukh: We can send traffic info early next week.

[20:35] Evan Lin: And I can send sample prompts for summarization.

[20:38] Sarah Nguyen: I’ll write down success criteria.

[20:41] Alex Martinez: Awesome.

[20:43] Sean Gallagher: I’ll draft the dashboard + alert spec for pilot and share. I want to avoid noisy paging on queue delay; we’ll do it carefully.

[20:54] Karthik Iyer: Thank you. That’s the part I care most about.

[21:00] Miguel Santos: Cool. Before we wrap, any other vendor comparisons we should know about? Just so we’re not missing something.

[21:07] Sarah Nguyen: We looked at Together for cost. And Bedrock for procurement reasons. But we need better observability; that’s the issue.

[21:16] Miguel Santos: Got it. We’ll lean into that in the pilot.

[21:21] Alex Martinez: Also, if you want to compare, we can set up an A/B with same model version and only change tier.

[21:28] Evan Lin: That’s ideal.

[21:31] Miguel Santos: Great. Let’s do a quick recap and next steps.

[21:36] Miguel Santos: Recap:
- We’ll start POC in Hosted.
- Tiers per route: fast for streaming chat, standard for embeddings and non-stream chat, cost-efficient for async summarization.
- Success metrics: TTFT/cadence for streaming, p95 latency + timeout/cancel rate, and $/1M tokens improvement for cost-efficient.
- Dashboards: latency by tier, queue delay, batch formation, errors, and (where available) GPU/memory signals.
- Rollout: staged, route-by-route, with pause/rollback triggers.

[22:12] Sarah Nguyen: Sounds right.

[22:14] Priya Deshmukh: Yep.

[22:15] Karthik Iyer: Works.

[22:17] Evan Lin: Yep, thanks.

[22:20] Miguel Santos: Cool. Alex will send the config snippets and a proposed tier matrix in email. Sean will send dashboard/alert proposal. Let’s schedule a check-in after the first benchmark run.

[22:32] Alex Martinez: I’ll include a note about effective config precedence too.

[22:36] Nikhil Sharma: And I’ll send the Hosted streaming metrics we expose today.

[22:40] Miguel Santos: Great. Thanks everyone.

[22:43] (Call continues with scheduling / calendar chatter, minor cross talk)

[23:05] Sarah Nguyen: Miguel, can you also send the security doc link? Our legal will ask.

[23:10] Miguel Santos: Yep, will do.

[23:12] Priya Deshmukh: And if possible, a one-pager on what “cost-efficient tier” actually changes.

[23:17] Alex Martinez: We have a docs page draft; I’ll send what we have. It explains the tradeoffs.

[23:23] Karthik Iyer: Please include the queue delay defaults, if you can.

[23:27] Sean Gallagher: We can share the target range, but we might tune based on your workload. We’ll document what’s effective.

[23:36] Karthik Iyer: That’s fine.

[23:38] Miguel Santos: Alright, thanks all.

(Recording ends.)
